Researcher and podcaster Lex Fridman returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2260. Fridman has visited the show many times over the years. He is known for long talks on science, tech, and human nature.

The sample opens with a crude physics joke from the crew. Fridman plays along before the talk turns to deeper ground. Past visits covered smart machines, love, and the mind. This one keeps the same loose, curious tone. Listeners who enjoy Rogan at his most open-ended will find a familiar, unhurried conversation with a trusted repeat guest.

Joe Rogan talks Peter Popoff, televangelists, and the Bible in a segment drawn from episode 350 of his show. Popoff is the faith healer caught in a famed scam in which an earpiece fed him facts he claimed God gave him. Rogan hosts the tour of fraud and faith.

Rogan works through how Popoff's act was built and how it was brought down. He then roams to the wider world of TV preachers and what the Bible truly says, as he reads it. The segment is an early, raw cut of the show. Listeners get Rogan young and blunt. The library holds the file as an archive record.

Author James Nestor joins Joe Rogan for episode 1506 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Nestor wrote Breath, the hit book on how we breathe and how it shapes health. His work sent him to labs, free divers, and monks.

Nestor and Rogan talk through the lost art of the breath: slow, through the nose, and with care. He shares the tests that showed him how much mouth breath harms sleep and mood. Rogan tries the tips as they talk. Listeners get a guide they can use the same day. The library keeps the episode as a record of a famed health talk.
podcast-joerogan-xiCcrk0eT2E:
Philosopher Philip Goff makes the case for panpsychism in episode 1739 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Goff argues in his book Galileo's Error that consciousness is not limited to brains. On his view, mind is a basic feature of matter itself, present everywhere in simple forms.

Goff explains why he thinks science cannot explain inner experience by matter alone. He walks Rogan through how tiny sparks of experience might combine into a human mind. Rogan tests the idea against rocks, plants, and machines. Thoughtful listeners get a clear, friendly tour of one of philosophy's boldest revivals.
podcast-tuckercarlson-7Ntn8ImrL2E:
Tucker Carlson and writer Charlie Spiering react to the Al Smith dinner, a set piece of campaign season. They start with how to say Kamala Harris's name. Old ads, they note, taught voters the sounds.

They joke that a wrong sound now draws charges of racism at once. From there they review the dinner's jokes and jabs. The title asks why Democrats turn against their own candidate. The pair argue her campaign strains even friendly crowds. The episode is a witty, close read of one night that reveals a party mood.
podcast-tuckercarlson-I3VPamDEU2E:
Commentator Auron MacIntyre tells Tucker Carlson that the American empire is racing toward collapse, and offers his guide to preventing it. MacIntyre, a dissident writer and video host, argues the country's institutions have hollowed out. His warning is stark, and his fixes are radical by mainstream lights.

MacIntyre lays out the decay he sees in law, money, and shared culture. He argues collapse can be slowed only by facing how power really works now. Carlson, who shares much of the diagnosis, asks what ordinary people should build instead. Prepared and concerned viewers get a dissident's manual for hard times.
